guide.title: Medication-Assisted Treatment
guide.lead: Many patients take medicines for opioid or alcohol use disorder. Know which ones block opioids, which ones partly replace them and which ones make alcohol dangerous – because they change how you treat overdose and pain. Speak with respect: these are patients in treatment.

sections.title: Opioid use disorder
rows: Overdose lasts long: repeated naloxone or infusion; QT prolongation
Overdose still possible with fentanyl, alcohol or benzodiazepines; may need higher or repeated naloxone. Pain: give analgesia – opioids still work at higher doses
Opioid analgesics won't work: use ketamine, NSAIDs, acetaminophen

sections.title: Alcohol use disorder
rows: Alcohol causes flushing, vomiting, chest pain, tachycardia, low BP: fluids, antiemetic, monitor

steps.title: Titrate naloxone
steps.text: Small doses to adequate breathing, not to full wakefulness.

steps.title: Precipitated withdrawal
steps.text: Vomiting, agitation, sweating, pain: protect the airway, antiemetic, calm de-escalation. It isn't life-threatening in adults but drives refusals.

steps.title: Leave naloxone and links
steps.text: Leave-behind naloxone and referral to treatment where your service offers it; some services start buprenorphine after reversal.

sections.title: Words matter
rows: Person with a substance use disorder

quiz.q: Man on buprenorphine-naloxone used heroin: unresponsive, RR 8, SpO₂ 86%. You:
options: Ventilate and give naloxone; higher or repeated doses may be needed
quiz.explanation: Buprenorphine doesn't prevent overdose with full agonists.

quiz.q: Patient on monthly naltrexone with renal colic wants pain relief. You know:
options: Opioids won't work: use non-opioids such as ketamine or NSAIDs

quiz.q: After 8 mg intranasal naloxone from family: awake, agitated, vomiting, sweating. Priority?
options: Precipitated withdrawal: protect the airway, antiemetic, de-escalate

quiz.q: Man with alcohol use disorder on a 'new medication for drinking', drank today, now flushed and vomiting. Key question?

options: A partial mu agonist with a ceiling effect
quiz.explanation: Limits breathing depression when taken alone.

quiz.q: Methadone overdose is a particular problem because:
options: It lasts much longer than naloxone
quiz.explanation: Repeated doses or infusion; observe in hospital.

options: Fluids, antiemetic, monitoring; vasopressors if needed

quiz.q: Patient on buprenorphine with appendicitis pain. You:
options: Treat the pain: ketamine or titrated opioids (may need higher doses)
quiz.explanation: Buprenorphine doesn't remove the need for analgesia.

flashcards.question: Buprenorphine ceiling effect
flashcards.answer: Higher doses add little effect, limiting breathing depression when taken alone – but full agonists still work at higher doses for pain.

flashcards.question: Precipitated withdrawal
flashcards.answer: Sudden withdrawal when naloxone or buprenorphine displaces a full agonist: vomiting, diarrhoea, pain, agitation, sweating. Supportive care.

flashcards.question: Can someone on buprenorphine overdose?
flashcards.answer: Yes: with fentanyl, alcohol, benzodiazepines, or if opioid-naive. Ventilate and give naloxone.

flashcards.question: Pain on naltrexone
flashcards.answer: Opioids are blocked. Use ketamine, NSAIDs, acetaminophen or regional anaesthesia.

flashcards.question: Disulfiram reaction
flashcards.answer: Alcohol plus disulfiram: flushing, headache, vomiting, chest pain, tachycardia, low BP. Fluids, antiemetic, monitor.

flashcards.question: Person-first language
flashcards.answer: "Person with a substance use disorder", "return to use", "positive/negative" – not "addict", "relapse", "dirty".

critical.scenario: 28-year-old stable on buprenorphine for 2 years: severe right lower abdominal pain, fever, guarding.
critical.question: Pain management?

options.t: Give analgesia: ketamine 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV, or titrated fentanyl (may need more than usual); ondansetron; transport
Tell her to take extra buprenorphine

critical.explanation: Tell the hospital so they continue her buprenorphine.
critical.kpi: Provides analgesia for a patient on buprenorphine

critical.scenario: 34-year-old stopped heroin 18 hours ago: vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps, sweating, dilated pupils, goosebumps, HR 124, distressed.
critical.question: Diagnosis and management?

options.t: Opioid withdrawal: supportive care (fluids, antiemetic), calm reassurance, transport or referral; buprenorphine per local protocol

options.f: Withdrawal drives return to use and dehydration.

critical.explanation: This is a chance to connect him with treatment.

critical.scenario: 52-year-old on disulfiram drank several beers 2 hours ago: flushing, headache, vomiting, chest tightness, HR 118, BP 86/52.
critical.question: Diagnosis and management?

options.t: Disulfiram reaction: oxygen, monitor and 12-lead, IV fluids, antiemetic, transport; vasopressors if hypotension persists

critical.explanation: Check the 12-lead: chest pain may be cardiac.
critical.kpi: Recognizes and manages a disulfiram-alcohol reaction
